questions.stem: Which combustion condition produces carbon monoxide in exhaust fumes?

options.text: A limited oxygen supply at the flame
options.explanation: Incomplete combustion leaves carbon half-oxidised.
Plentiful oxygen drives carbon to carbon dioxide.
Temperature outdoors does not create CO at the flame.
The converter destroys CO; it does not create it.

questions.stem: Why is carbon monoxide toxic to humans?

options.explanation: Inhalation, not ingestion, is the exposure route.

options.text: It binds to haemoglobin in place of oxygen, preventing oxygen transport
options.explanation: The occupancy blocks the blood's delivery system.

options.text: It burns the lungs on contact
options.explanation: CO is not corrosive.

options.text: It dissolves the red blood cells
options.explanation: The cells persist; their cargo sites are blocked.

questions.stem: Why do victims often fail to notice carbon monoxide exposure?

options.explanation: The danger is precisely the absence of pain.

options.text: It is visible as a haze
options.explanation: It is invisible.

options.text: The gas is colourless and odourless
options.explanation: No sensory cue accompanies the poisoning.
No taste cue exists.

questions.stem: Which statement about CO and haemoglobin is correct?

options.explanation: The opposite: CO wins the binding contest.
It prevents transport entirely.

options.text: The binding is reversible within seconds harmlessly
options.explanation: The persistence is what makes exposure dangerous.

options.text: CO's binding to haemoglobin is stronger than oxygen's
options.explanation: Preferential occupancy is the toxicity engine.

questions.stem: How is carbon monoxide formation best prevented at the source?

options.text: Ensure complete combustion with adequate oxygen supply
options.explanation: Plenty of air keeps carbon on the CO2 route.
Sulfur adds its own pollution problems.
CO forms at the flame, not the pipe.
The air supply quantity, not its filtration, decides the combustion completeness.

questions.stem: State where carbon monoxide forms and the property that makes it dangerous.
questions.modelAnswer: It forms in the incomplete combustion of alkane fuels when oxygen is limited, and it is toxic because it prevents oxygen transport by occupying haemoglobin.

questions.stem: Explain the haemoglobin mechanism in two sentences.
questions.modelAnswer: Carbon monoxide binds to haemoglobin more strongly than oxygen does; the occupied sites cannot carry oxygen, so the blood's delivery capacity falls.

questions.stem: Explain why the phrase 'silent killer' is chemically justified for CO.
questions.modelAnswer: Both hazard channels run silent: the gas gives no colour or smell warning, and its binding displaces oxygen without any immediate sensation, so harm arrives before detection.

questions.stem: A garage runs an engine with the door closed. Explain the hazard in mechanism terms and give the condition that would remove it.
questions.modelAnswer: The restricted-air flame forms carbon monoxide, which on inhalation occupies haemoglobin sites and blocks oxygen transport; ensuring complete combustion through adequate ventilation and air supply removes the formation condition.

questions.stem: What is the source of sulfur dioxide in exhaust emissions?

options.explanation: Converters reduce pollutants; they do not emit sulfur dioxide.

options.text: Sulfur impurities burned within the fossil fuel
options.explanation: The alkane fuel carries trace sulfur that oxidises.
Alkanes are hydrocarbons - no sulfur in the chain.
Nitrogen yields the nitrogen oxides, not sulfur dioxide.

questions.stem: How do oxides of nitrogen form inside an engine?

options.explanation: Oil is not the nitrogen source.

options.text: Nitrogen monoxide is added to petrol
options.explanation: No such additive exists.

options.text: Nitrogen and oxygen from air combine at the high flame temperature
options.explanation: Heat gives the normally inert nitrogen its chance to react.

options.text: Nitrogen impurities in the fuel burn
options.explanation: Fuel-borne nitrogen is not the mechanism.

questions.stem: What environmental damage do both oxide families share?

options.text: They deplete the ozone layer directly
options.explanation: Ozone chemistry is a different concern.
That is carbon monoxide's mechanism.
Sea level is not the acid-rain damage.
Both dissolve into acidic solutions in atmospheric moisture.

questions.stem: Which statement correctly pairs sulfur dioxide and the nitrogen oxides with their origins?

options.text: Sulfur dioxide - sulfur impurity combustion; nitrogen oxides - air at flame temperature
options.explanation: Each source is correctly assigned.

options.text: Sulfur dioxide - air at flame temperature; nitrogen oxides - fuel impurities
options.explanation: The pairing is exactly reversed.

options.text: Sulfur dioxide - the alkane chain; nitrogen oxides - the alkane chain
options.explanation: Alkanes contain neither sulfur nor nitrogen.

options.text: Sulfur dioxide - rainwater; nitrogen oxides - rainwater
options.explanation: Rain is the victim, not the origin.

questions.stem: Why does high engine temperature matter for nitrogen oxide formation?

options.text: The converter needs heat to make NOx
options.explanation: Converters destroy NOx; the engine makes it.

options.text: Only at high temperature does nitrogen react with oxygen
options.explanation: The normally inert N2 triple bond needs the energy input.
Nitrogen is stable; the reactivity appears with heat.
Dissolution is not the relevant chemistry.

questions.stem: Name the two oxide families that cause acid rain from combustion.
questions.modelAnswer: Oxides of sulfur (chiefly sulfur dioxide) and oxides of nitrogen (such as nitrogen monoxide and nitrogen dioxide).

questions.stem: State the origin of each oxide family in two phrases.
questions.modelAnswer: Sulfur dioxide arises from burning sulfur impurities in fuels; nitrogen oxides arise when air's nitrogen and oxygen combine at engine temperatures.

questions.stem: Explain why the nitrogen oxides problem cannot be solved by cleaning the fuel.
questions.modelAnswer: The nitrogen does not ride in the fuel at all - it comes from the air the engine breathes, so fuel treatment cannot touch it and only engine-side technology can.

questions.stem: A power station burns coal with significant sulfur content. Name the primary pollutant gas, its atmospheric fate and one removal strategy.
questions.modelAnswer: Sulfur dioxide is the pollutant; it dissolves in atmospheric moisture to give acidic rain, and flue-gas desulfurisation with a basic absorbent removes it before release.

questions.stem: Which device treats both carbon monoxide and nitrogen monoxide in exhaust fumes?

options.explanation: That removes particulates.
That targets sulfur dioxide.
The converter converts the pair into carbon dioxide and nitrogen.
Scrubbers serve power-station sulfur dioxide.

questions.stem: What does a catalytic converter turn 2CO + 2NO into?

options.explanation: Nitrogen must leave as N2, not another oxide.
Carbon departs as CO2.
The reactant cannot reappear as the product.
Both toxics are converted into harmless products.

questions.stem: Which absorbent class removes sulfur dioxide in flue-gas desulfurisation?

options.text: A basic absorbent such as calcium carbonate
options.explanation: Acidic SO2 meets a base and is captured.
Acid does not neutralise acid.
Radicals belong to the UV substitution topic.
Nickel serves hydrogenation chemistry.

questions.stem: Why must pollutant removal methods be matched to their site?

options.explanation: They need exhaust gases, which vehicles supply.

options.text: Converters work on vehicle exhausts while scrubbers work on power-station flue gases
options.explanation: Each technology fits its emission source.
The site-specific design contradicts this.
Practicality, not legality, is the reason they do not pair.

questions.stem: Which pollutant-and-effect row is correct?

options.explanation: The opposite of the acid effect.
Acidity belongs to the oxide rows.

options.text: Carbon monoxide - toxic because it prevents oxygen transport
options.explanation: The haemoglobin mechanism is the effect.
That is carbon monoxide's row.

questions.stem: State the equation the catalytic converter uses to remove CO and NO together.
questions.modelAnswer: 2CO + 2NO -> 2CO2 + N2, converting both toxics into harmless products.

questions.stem: Name one removal method for sulfur dioxide from power-station emissions.
questions.modelAnswer: Flue-gas desulfurisation, scrubbing the gas with a basic absorbent such as calcium carbonate.

questions.stem: Explain why the converter's products are acceptable while its reactants are not.
questions.modelAnswer: Carbon dioxide and nitrogen are the normal constituents of air and breath, whereas carbon monoxide poisons blood and nitrogen oxides acidify rain - the converter trades two toxics for two natural gases.

questions.stem: A table row lists a gas removed by calcium carbonate scrubbing. Name the gas, its combustion origin and the balanced scrubbing equation.
questions.modelAnswer: The gas is sulfur dioxide, formed when sulfur impurities in fuel burn; the scrubbing capture runs CaCO3 + SO2 -> CaSO3 + CO2, storing the sulfur as solid sulfite.
